messages.subject: Re: Multivariate GWAS to identify differences
messages.body_plain:
Hi Helen,

Just to summarize, it sounds like you have a set of 5 traits that you know generally conform to a common factor model, but given some unique genetic variance for each trait, you want to identify individual genetic variants that are trait-specific? In this case, your easiest path forward would be to run the commonfactor function just to confirm that this model fits the data well and then, as you say, use the Q-statistic that is automatically output by the commonfactorGWAS function to identifying different variants that do not conform to this common factor structure.

As far as what to do with binary traits where the prevalences are not known I would say you can either put in NA as you say (not ideal but if you have no other information what can you do) or take a best guess as far as the population prevalence. In many cases, the literature will report somewhat varied population prevalences depending on the given trait, but within a range of .05 that isn't going to drastically change your results. I would also say I have yet to come across a set of summary statistics where I can't get the sample prevalence for the simple reason that I don't think a GWAS could get published without reporting the split of cases and controls somewhere in the paper. Of course, this may be a very unique case where this information is not available, and again I would put in NAs for both sample and population prevalence if that is the case. Hope this helps, but of course post any follow-up questions this may raise if anything is unclear!

Best,
  Andrew

messages.subject: Re: GWAS-by-subtraction
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joan,

The output from the GWAS commands should match with respect to number of SNPs with output from the sumstats file. For runs that did not converge, or failed in some way, the function should print rows with those warnings and error messages so even in these cases you should have ended up with 8378151 SNPs. If you are running the multivariate GWAS using serial processing, the functions will print intermittent updates with respect to what model it is on (e.g., "Running Model 10,000) for every 1,000 runs. If you are using parallel processing, unfortunately the package doesn't print any updates at the current moment because the different cores may be on different runs and you would just end up getting a bunch of garbled output the way things are currently coded. Are you using serial or parallel processing?

On the computer clusters I use, if the cluster runs out of memory the job will typically fail without saving any of the output, so I've also never run into a situation where it saves partial output at the point it runs out of memory. However, this could be a cluster specific feature so running out of memory seems like a likely explanation. Since all multivariate GWAS runs are entirely independent of one another, my suggestion would be to split up the output from sumstats in some way (by chromosome, or in even chunks) and try re-running to see if the output ends early, or the same SNPs are excluded from your output.

Best,
-Andrew

messages.body_plain:
Hi Helen,

Apologies for the delays in getting back to you! It looks like the problem was that a common factor model for your particular set of variables produces a negative residual variance for V1. In the context of the commonfactorGWAS, certain runs were producing way out of bounds estimates that were causing the function to break, which is why you were able to re-run for some subsets of SNPs but not others. I've put in a patch on the github so that the function will still return estimates, but you'll see that you get a warning about the negative residual variance. As you may know, you shouldn't interpret the estimates from a model with negative residuals.

I also tried running a model on just the LDSC covariance matrix in which the residuals are constrained, and find that this fits the data OK, but not great. When running the userGWAS function with these same constraints to keep the residuals above 0, you get a lot of errors and warnings, many of which are about the variance covariance matrix producing eigenvalues below 0. In my experience, eigenvalues near 0 seem to be acceptable, but below 0 tends to produce estimates that are very inconsistent across the genome, with manhattan plots that don't look sensible. I've attached a script with the steps I took if you want to take a look, and would just note that if you re-install GenomicSEM with the commonfactorGWAS patch that you should restart R after installing to make sure the updated version of GenomicSEM is loaded. Unfortunately, it seems that a common factor model ultimately does not describe the data you are working with very well. Your options could be to subset to a smaller set of variables, include additional variables, or consider specifying an alternative model. Hope this helps and course let me know if this raises any follow-up questions.

I determined this after I saw the warning from the GWAS function, and then ran the commonfactor function to see which variable was producing the negative residual. I then specified a usermodel with a constraint on that particular residual, which seems to produce sensible output. Finally, I ran userGWAS on a subset of SNPs just to see if that output also seemed sensible, and it seems to be running without any errors or warning at least for the handful I ran through. Hope this helps and let me know if you end up having any more issues or questions!

a > .001"

F1~SNP

OwnBW~~a*OwnBW

a > .001"
